Book 5. By the Rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137). old version, quote family, public edition. Sixteen complete quote books in the Library of Jerusalem, old version: short cited King James Version excerpts with commentary chapters, read aloud by Anonymous of Peace.

Preface to the public edition (commentary): this public edition of By the Rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137) presents the passage cited as Psalm 137:1 with commentary chapters written for every reader. The commentary studies the quoted words, sets them in their time, surveys how readers have heard them, and draws design lessons, ceremonies, festivals, and a rebuild guide from them. The theme of this book is exile, memory, and longing for Zion, and the study image that guides it is willows hanging over a slow river far from home. Read the quoted words first, then the commentary, keeping the boundary between them clear throughout.

Chapter 1 — Opening the Book: First Reading. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

This book, By the Rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137), opens with a single short passage and a long study. The passage is cited as Psalm 137:1, and it is quoted in full at the head of every chapter so that the reader never has to guess which words are being studied and which words are commentary about them. The theme of the whole book is exile, memory, and longing for Zion, and every chapter returns to that theme from a different direction: first by reading, then by weighing words, then by setting the passage in its time, then by hearing how readers have heard it, then by drawing design lessons, ceremonies, and a rebuild guide from it. The book is written so that a reader who opens it at any chapter can still find the quoted words, the citation, and the boundary between quotation and commentary stated plainly. In the public edition, this lesson is offered as a study proposal drawn from the cited words, open to every reader, and offered as a design study, never as a claim about a built structure. The reading room imagined for this book holds 6 study rooms and 60 reading seats, a scale chosen for study on paper, not a claim about any built place.

The quoted words for this book are short on purpose. A short excerpt can be read slowly, word by word, without losing the thread of the sentence, and a short excerpt keeps the commentary honest: the commentary must earn its length by saying something true about a small text, rather than by hiding behind a long one. In this opening chapter the reader is asked to read the excerpt aloud once, then silently once, then to name the single word that catches their attention first. That word becomes a thread to follow through the rest of the book, because the same word will return in the word study, in the history, in the ceremonies, and in the rebuild guide, each time carrying a little more weight. The image that guides this book is willows hanging over a slow river far from home, and the reader should hold that image lightly, as a study picture, while reading. Nothing in this book describes a built city, and nothing here should be read as a report on construction.

By the end of this opening chapter the reader should be able to do three things without help: state the citation of the passage, repeat the quoted words accurately, and explain in one sentence what exile, memory, and longing for Zion means in this book. The chapters that follow build on those three abilities in order. The word study slows the reading down. The history widens it. The interpretation chapters test it against other readings. The design chapters turn it into rooms, materials, and light on paper. The ceremonies and festivals turn it into shared practice. The rebuild guide turns it into a plan that can be checked, corrected, and kept. Each step is commentary, and each step says so, so that the quoted words themselves remain exactly as cited, unchanged by anything the commentary adds around them.

Read the quoted words aloud once, then silently once, and write down the single word that catches your attention first, with one sentence saying why it caught you.

State the citation, Psalm 137:1, from memory, and check it against the head of this chapter, correcting any error before moving on.

Describe exile, memory, and longing for Zion in one sentence of your own, without quoting the passage again, and keep that sentence beside you for the rest of the book.

Picture willows hanging over a slow river far from home as a study image only, and note in writing that it is a design picture, not a report on a built place.

Count the study rooms and reading seats named for this book, 6 rooms and 60 seats, and ask what a room of that size would need for light, air, and quiet.

Write down one question the passage leaves you with, to carry into the word study of the next chapter, and leave it unanswered for now.

Chapter 2 — Word Study: Weighing Each Word. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

This chapter weighs the quoted words one at a time, because a short passage repays slow reading. The commentary here works through the sentence structure first: which words carry the action, which words set the condition, and which words name the promise or the warning. Then it turns to the nouns, because the nouns decide what the reader pictures: willows hanging over a slow river far from home is the picture this book works with, and each noun in the passage either supports that picture or corrects it. A word study does not change the quoted words; it changes the reader, by making the familiar words strange again for long enough to see them clearly. In the public edition, this lesson is offered as a study proposal drawn from the cited words, open to every reader, and offered as a design study, never as a claim about a built structure.

Three habits govern this word study. First, compare the word as used here with the same word as used in ordinary speech, and notice where the passage stretches ordinary use. Second, ask what the sentence would lose if that word were removed, because the words that cannot be removed without collapsing the sentence are the load-bearing words. Third, ask what the passage does not say: the silences around a short excerpt are part of its meaning, and a careful reader marks them instead of filling them with guesses. Applied to exile, memory, and longing for Zion, these habits show that the passage says less than a hasty reading assumes, and more than a careless reading notices, which is why the study takes a whole chapter for a few dozen words.

The result of this chapter is a small glossary the reader has written for themselves: each load-bearing word of the passage, in their own words, with the citation beside it. That glossary travels with the reader into the history chapter, where the same words will be heard in their own time, and into the design chapters, where the same words will be turned into river willow and clay and memory, lament, and return on paper. A glossary written by hand is worth more than one copied, because the act of paraphrasing forces the reader to decide what they actually understand. Where understanding fails, the glossary should say so plainly, because an honest gap is better than a smooth paraphrase that hides ignorance.

List every noun in the quoted words, and beside each one write whether it supports the picture of willows hanging over a slow river far from home or corrects it, with one reason.

Find the load-bearing words of the passage by removing each word in turn and noting which removals collapse the sentence.

Write a one-sentence paraphrase of the passage in your own words, labeled commentary, and check that no quoted wording has slipped into it unmarked.

Name one thing the passage does not say about exile, memory, and longing for Zion, and mark it as a silence to respect, not a gap to fill with a guess.

Connect one word of the passage to river willow and clay, and explain in two sentences whether that connection is in the text or is a design reading added by commentary.

Keep your glossary for this book in one place, and bring it to every later chapter, adding to it rather than rewriting it.

Chapter 3 — The Passage in Its Own Time. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

A passage is never heard in a vacuum, and this chapter sets the quoted words in their own time so that the reader does not mistake a modern picture for an ancient one. The world behind these words was a world of memory, lament, and return in daily life, of roads, markets, courts, and houses built from river willow and clay, and of listeners who heard the words spoken aloud rather than reading them silently from a page. Hearing the words as spoken, to people who lived under particular rulers, taxes, customs, and hopes, changes their weight: a blessing, a warning, or a promise lands differently when the listener's daily bread, safety, and standing are at stake. This chapter is commentary throughout, drawn from the general historical setting of the passage, and it never presents a guess about a particular day or place as if it were recorded fact.

The setting matters for exile, memory, and longing for Zion because the theme itself was first heard as news, not as theory. Listeners who heard about willows hanging over a slow river far from home would have pictured something from their own surroundings, not from a modern city plan, and the commentary must respect that distance. When the passage speaks of gates, tables, roads, or houses, the history chapter asks what those things meant to the first hearers: who could pass through a gate, who sat at a table, who walked a road safely, and who did not. Those questions keep the reading honest, because they stop the modern reader from importing modern comforts, modern maps, and modern institutions into an old sentence and then congratulating the sentence for agreeing with them.

At the same time, history does not imprison the passage. A text that could only mean what it meant on its first hearing would be a curiosity, not a book to live with, and the later chapters of this book will show how the same words have been read, prayed, built from, and argued over across centuries. But the order matters: first hearing before later hearings, first setting before later settings, so that every later reading can be measured against the first one and shown to be a development, a correction, or a departure. The reader who skips the history chapter will still enjoy the design chapters, but will not know which parts of the design come from the text and which parts come from the designer, and that distinction is the whole discipline of this book.

Describe the daily world behind the passage in five sentences, using only general historical facts about roads, markets, courts, and houses of the time.

Explain how a first hearer might have pictured willows hanging over a slow river far from home, and how that picture differs from a modern picture of the same words.

Ask who could pass, sit, walk, or enter in the world of the passage, and who could not, and note what that says about exile, memory, and longing for Zion.

Mark every sentence in this chapter that is a general historical claim, and separate it from any sentence that is a guess, labeling the guess as a guess.

Write down one way the historical setting corrects a modern reading of the passage, in two sentences.

Bring your glossary from the word study into this chapter, and add a historical note beside each load-bearing word.

Chapter 4 — How Readers Have Heard These Words. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

After the first hearing comes the long history of hearings, and this chapter surveys how readers have heard these words across time, without pretending that every hearing agrees. Some readers have heard the passage as comfort, some as challenge, some as a rule for building a community, and some as a warning against building one. The commentary here does not adjudicate every dispute, because a quote book that settled all disputes would be a creed, not a study. Instead it names the main lines of reading, shows what each line emphasizes in the quoted words, and lets the reader see why a single short passage can sustain readings that pull in different directions. All of this is commentary, and none of it changes the quoted words.

The value of hearing many readings is that it exposes the reader's own first reading as one reading among others, not as the obvious meaning. A reader who has only ever heard exile, memory, and longing for Zion in one key will hear this chapter as a widening: the same words, heard by farmers, by city dwellers, by scholars, by prisoners, and by builders, sound different in each mouth, and each hearing reveals something the others miss. The discipline is to listen without immediately choosing a winner, to note which words each reading leans on, and to ask what each reading costs: what it must downplay in the passage to make its case. A reading that costs nothing, that explains everything smoothly, should be suspected, because short passages resist smooth explanations.

This chapter closes by returning the reader to their own hearing, now informed rather than merely initial. The reader is asked to restate their own reading of exile, memory, and longing for Zion in light of the readings surveyed, keeping what survives, dropping what does not, and marking what remains uncertain. Uncertainty is not failure here; it is the honest state of a reader who has listened widely and still finds the passage larger than any one reading. The design chapters that follow will draw on this widened hearing, and they will be stronger for it, because a design drawn from a narrow hearing is a narrow design, while a design drawn from a wide hearing has room for many kinds of people.

Name three different ways readers have heard this passage, and for each one state which words of the passage it leans on most heavily.

For each of those readings, state what it must downplay in the passage to make its case, in one sentence each.

Restate your own reading of exile, memory, and longing for Zion after this survey, keeping what survives and dropping what does not, with reasons.

Mark one question about the passage that remains uncertain after listening widely, and keep it open rather than forcing an answer.

Explain how a widened hearing changes the design picture of willows hanging over a slow river far from home, in two sentences.

Note which reading of the passage you find most challenging, and why, without dismissing it.

Chapter 5 — First Design Lesson: Shaping a Room. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

The first design lesson turns the passage into a room on paper. The room is willows hanging over a slow river far from home, and the lesson is that a room shaped by exile, memory, and longing for Zion must be judged by the passage, not by fashion. A room for this theme needs 6 study rooms in the plan and 60 reading seats, not because those numbers are in the passage, for they are not, but because a design study needs concrete numbers to test itself against, and these numbers are stated here as study numbers, chosen for this book, so that the reader can check the plan rather than merely admire it. The room is drawn with river willow and clay and arranged under the system of memory, lament, and return, and every choice in the drawing is labeled as a design choice made by commentary, not as a fact stated by the passage.

The test of the room is use. Imagine a stranger entering the room for the first time: where do they sit, what do they see first, where do they go for water, for quiet, for help, and where does the room fail them? A room that serves only the confident, only the strong, or only the already convinced has failed the test of this passage, whatever its beauty. The design lesson therefore works backwards from failure: list the ways the room could exclude, confuse, or tire its visitors, and correct the drawing before praising it. This is the discipline that separates a design study from a fantasy, because a fantasy hides its failures while a study exhibits them and corrects them on paper, where correction costs nothing.

An inline diagram accompanies this chapter in the book page, drawn in lines and shapes rather than in any pictured likeness, showing the arrangement of the room in plan: entry, seats, light, and passage. The diagram is a study aid, not a blueprint for building, and it carries the same boundary as the whole book: the full-scale build is not established, and any large figure used elsewhere in this suite is illustrative only. The reader is invited to redraw the diagram with corrections, because a diagram that cannot be corrected is a monument, while a diagram that invites correction is a tool, and this book is a tool for study.

Draw the room of willows hanging over a slow river far from home in plan on paper, marking entry, seats, light, and passage, and label the drawing as a design study.

Walk a stranger through your drawing in writing, naming where they sit, what they see first, and where they go for water, quiet, and help.

List three ways your room could exclude, confuse, or tire a visitor, and correct the drawing for each one.

State which choices in your drawing come from the passage and which come from commentary, in two separate lists.

Check your room against exile, memory, and longing for Zion in one paragraph: does the room serve the theme, or merely decorate it?

Redraw one part of the room after the failure test, and note what changed and why.

Chapter 6 — Second Design Lesson: Materials and Light. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

The second design lesson turns to materials and light, because a room is not only a shape but a substance and a brightness. The materials chosen for this book are river willow and clay, and the light imagined for it is the light that serves exile, memory, and longing for Zion: light that lets a reader see the page, a visitor see the way, and a gathering see one another's faces. Materials are never neutral: stone says permanence, timber says warmth and repair, glass says openness and fragility, and each material brings its own costs in weight, in care, and in replacement. The commentary here weighs those costs openly, because a design that hides its material costs is a promise it cannot keep, while a design that states them can be judged honestly.

Light deserves its own study because so much of this book's theme depends on seeing clearly. A room lit only from above feels watched; a room lit only from the side feels divided; a room with no dark corners feels safe but also exposed, and a room with deep shadows feels private but also unsafe. The lesson therefore plans light in layers: daylight for the main hours, lamp light for the evening, and small lights for paths and thresholds, so that no visitor must cross darkness to reach help. This is a design reading, labeled as such, drawn from the passage by commentary, and it is offered for study on paper, not as a specification for any built work. Where the passage speaks of light, the commentary says so; where it does not, the commentary owns the addition.

The materials and light of this book also teach care: every material chosen must be maintainable by ordinary hands with ordinary tools, or the design has failed the people who must live with it. A material that only specialists can repair makes its users dependent, while a material that a household can mend makes its users capable, and capability is part of exile, memory, and longing for Zion in this book. The reader is asked to choose one material in the plan and to write its full care story: where it comes from, how it is worked, how it fails, how it is mended, and what it costs over a lifetime of use. A material without a care story is not a choice but a wish.

List the materials of this book, river willow and clay, and for each one write its weight, its care needs, and its failure mode in one sentence each.

Plan light for the room in three layers, daylight, lamp light, and path lights, and state what each layer is for.

Choose one material and write its full care story, from source to working to failure to mending to lifetime cost.

Find one place in your plan where a material choice was made for beauty alone, and either justify it or change it.

Explain in two sentences how the light plan serves exile, memory, and longing for Zion, and where the passage supports it versus where commentary adds it.

Name one material you would refuse for this room, and give the reason in terms of care, cost, or exclusion.

Chapter 7 — A Ceremony of Reading. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

A book that is only read alone is only half a book, and this chapter gives the book a ceremony of reading: a lament beside the river at evening. A ceremony is a shared way of doing a simple thing with attention, and the ceremony of reading in this book has four movements: gathering, silence, reading aloud, and silence again. The gathering brings readers together without hurry. The first silence lets each reader arrive. The reading aloud lets the quoted words be heard in a human voice, slowly, with pauses at the punctuation. The final silence lets the words settle before commentary begins, because commentary that rushes in too quickly drowns the text it claims to serve. The ceremony is a practice proposed by this book, not a rite claimed from any authority, and it is offered for any group that wishes to try it.

The ceremony works because it slows down the fastest readers and gives the slowest readers room. In ordinary reading, the quick finish first and the slow feel left behind, but in a ceremony of reading, everyone hears the same words at the same pace, and the pauses belong to everyone equally. The reader who leads the ceremony is asked to read as plainly as possible, without performance, because performance draws attention to the reader while plain reading draws attention to the words. After the reading, the ceremony allows one round of short responses, each no longer than a sentence, so that every voice is heard before the longer discussion begins, and no single voice can take the whole hour.

The ceremony of reading also protects the boundary of this book. Because the quoted words are read aloud first, and the commentary is labeled as commentary afterwards, no listener can mistake a comment for a quotation, and no leader can smuggle an opinion into the text by reading it in the same tone. The ceremony therefore ends with a spoken reminder: the words just heard are cited, the words that follow are commentary, and the difference matters. A group that keeps that reminder will read honestly even when it disagrees, and a group that drops it will soon argue about words that were never in the passage at all, which is the most common failure of shared reading.

Practise the ceremony of reading, a lament beside the river at evening, with at least two other people, following the four movements of gathering, silence, reading aloud, and silence again.

Read the quoted words aloud plainly, without performance, pausing at the punctuation, and note how plain reading changes what listeners hear.

After the reading, hold one round of one-sentence responses, so that every voice is heard before longer discussion begins.

Speak the boundary reminder aloud at the end of the ceremony: quoted words are cited, commentary is commentary, and the difference matters.

Write down one thing the ceremony revealed about exile, memory, and longing for Zion that silent reading alone had not revealed.

Adapt the ceremony for a single reader alone, keeping the silences, and note what is lost and what is kept.

Chapter 8 — A Ceremony of Welcome. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

Beside the ceremony of reading stands a ceremony of welcome, because a book about exile, memory, and longing for Zion must also say how a stranger is received. The ceremony of welcome in this book is simple: the door is opened before the stranger knocks twice, a seat is offered before a name is asked, water is given before business is discussed, and the quoted words are read aloud before any rule of the house is explained. The order matters, because a house that explains its rules before offering water has already told the stranger where they stand, while a house that offers water first has told them something better. This ceremony is proposed by commentary as a design for hospitality, not claimed as an ancient rite, and any group may adapt it to its own place and means.

Welcome is tested by its hardest case, not its easiest. It is easy to welcome a friend, a relative, or a person who already agrees; it is hard to welcome a person who is tired, dusty, late, or wrong, and the ceremony is written for the hard case. The host is asked to prepare the seat, the water, and the reading before the guest arrives, so that welcome does not depend on the host's mood on the day, and the guest is asked for nothing in return, because a welcome that demands payment, agreement, or gratitude in advance is a bargain, not a welcome. The ceremony therefore has a rule of no return: the host gives, the guest receives, and the account is closed by the giving itself, which is why the ceremony can be repeated without keeping score.

The ceremony of welcome also shapes the room. A room that welcomes well has its entry visible from the road, its seats near the door rather than hidden at the back, its water within reach, and its light bright enough that a stranger can see faces rather than shadows. The design chapters of this book return to these details, because hospitality is not only a feeling but a floor plan, and a floor plan that hides its entry, rations its seats, or darkens its corners has already refused the welcome its words profess. The reader is asked to test their own room against this ceremony, and to correct the plan where the room and the ceremony disagree, because the disagreement is the lesson.

Perform the ceremony of welcome for a real or imagined stranger, following the order of door, seat, water, and reading, and note where the order felt difficult.

Write the hardest case for welcome in your own place, a tired, late, or disagreeing stranger, and plan the ceremony for that case specifically.

Check the room of willows hanging over a slow river far from home against the ceremony: is the entry visible, are seats near the door, is water within reach, is light bright enough for faces?

State the rule of no return in your own words, and explain why a welcome that demands return is a bargain rather than a welcome.

Adapt the ceremony for a household with very little, naming what is kept when water, seats, or time are scarce.

Note one way your own place already welcomes well, and one way it fails, and correct the failing on paper before the next chapter.

Chapter 9 — A Day Shaped by the Saying. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

A saying that shapes only ceremonies will fade, and a saying that shapes only buildings will harden, so this chapter follows the saying into an ordinary day. The day shaped by exile, memory, and longing for Zion begins before dawn with quiet, moves into work done without hurry, pauses at midday for the shared table, returns to work in the afternoon, gathers at evening for reading, and ends with the blessing of peace before sleep. The hours are not a rule but a rhythm, and the rhythm is offered as a design for a day, not as a law for every life, because lives differ in work, in health, and in care for others, and a rhythm that cannot bend will break the people it claims to serve. The chapter is commentary throughout, and it invites the reader to test the rhythm for a single day rather than to adopt it for life.

The test of a day is its interruptions. A day that only works when nothing goes wrong is a picture, not a plan, so this chapter plans for the interruption explicitly: the visitor who arrives at midday, the work that runs long, the child who needs attention, the news that darkens the evening. In each case the rhythm bends in the same way: the shared table is kept, the reading is shortened rather than skipped, and the blessing of peace is spoken even when the day has gone badly, because a blessing spoken only on good days is a report on the weather, not a practice. The reader who tries the day will learn more from its first interruption than from its first success, and that learning is the point of the chapter.

The day also teaches the scale of this book. The study numbers of this book, 6 rooms and 60 seats, are the scale of a household and a neighbourhood, not of an empire, and the day described here fits that scale: a table, a room, a street, a well. A saying that promises to reshape the world in a day is selling something, while a saying that reshapes one day, repeated, reshapes a life without fanfare, and a life reshaped without fanfare reshapes a street, and a street reshapes a city, slowly enough to last. The chapter therefore ends where it began, in quiet, because the quiet at the end of a day is the measure of whether the day was shaped well.

Try the rhythm of this chapter for a single day, keeping the shared table, a shortened reading, and the evening blessing, and write down what happened.

Plan for three interruptions in advance, a visitor, work running long, and bad news, and state how the rhythm bends for each without breaking.

Describe your own ordinary day in five sentences, and mark where exile, memory, and longing for Zion already shapes it and where it does not.

Explain why the scale of this book, 6 rooms and 60 seats, fits a household and a neighbourhood rather than an empire.

Keep the evening blessing even on a bad day, and write one sentence about what changed when you did.

Adapt the rhythm for a person whose work is at night, keeping the table, the reading, and the blessing in a different order.

Chapter 10 — A Festival in the City. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

After the ordinary day comes the festival, because a community that never celebrates will forget what it values, and a community that only celebrates will forget how to work. The festival of this book is a day of remembrance for exiles, and it is planned as a day when the whole street, not only the household, gathers around exile, memory, and longing for Zion. The festival has a morning of preparation, a midday of shared food, an afternoon of stories and songs from the book, and an evening of light, and each part is open to strangers without fee, test, or prior agreement, because a festival that charges at the gate is a market, not a festival. The festival is a design proposed by commentary, offered for any community that wishes to adapt it, and it claims no ancient authority for its particular shape.

The festival teaches by doing what the chapters teach by saying. In the morning, households prepare food together, and the preparation itself is the lesson: many hands, shared work, no single cook taking the credit. At midday, the tables are joined into one long table, and seating is mixed so that neighbours sit beside strangers, because a festival that seats friends together merely repeats the ordinary divisions of the street. In the afternoon, the quoted words are read aloud, and the stories of the book are told in plain language for children and newcomers, so that no one needs prior learning to belong. In the evening, lights are lit along the street, and the festival ends with the same blessing of peace that ends an ordinary day, so that the festival and the day rhyme.

A festival also needs its limits, and this chapter states them plainly. The festival lasts one day, not a week, because a longer festival exhausts its hosts and becomes a burden disguised as a gift. The festival uses what the community already has, rather than borrowing splendour it cannot afford, because debt taken for a festival is paid long after the lights go out. The festival leaves the street cleaner than it found it, because a celebration that leaves mess for others has celebrated at their expense. These limits are part of the design, not an afterthought, and a community that keeps them will be able to celebrate again next year, which is the real test of a festival.

Plan a day of remembrance for exiles for your own street, with morning preparation, midday shared food, afternoon stories, and evening light, and state the cost of each part.

Seat neighbours beside strangers at the long table, and explain in two sentences why mixed seating matters for exile, memory, and longing for Zion.

Tell the story of this book in plain language for a child or newcomer, in five sentences, without using any unexplained special term.

State the three limits of the festival, one day, existing means, and a cleaner street, and explain what each limit protects.

Invite a stranger to the festival in writing, with no fee, test, or prior agreement required, and keep the invitation.

After the festival, write down what it taught about exile, memory, and longing for Zion that the chapters alone had not taught.

Chapter 11 — Keeping the Place in Repair. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

Festivals end, and ordinary days return, and the question then is how a place is kept rather than how it is built. This chapter is about care and repair for willows hanging over a slow river far from home, and its first claim is that repair is more honourable than novelty: a community that mends its tables, relights its lamps, and repoints its stonework is practising exile, memory, and longing for Zion more truly than a community that replaces everything at the first sign of wear. The materials of this book, river willow and clay, were chosen partly for this reason, because each of them can be mended by ordinary hands, and a material that cannot be mended makes its users into beggars for specialists. Care is therefore not housekeeping added to the design; care is the design, continued over time.

The care plan for this book has a yearly round. In spring, the roofs, channels, and drains are checked, because water is the patient enemy of every building. In summer, the timber and cloth are checked, because heat and insects work quietly. In autumn, the lamps, doors, and hinges are checked, because the dark season will test them nightly. In winter, the stores, fuel, and quiet rooms are checked, because a community is judged by how it shelters its weakest members in the hardest season. Each check is written down, with the date, the fault found, and the mending done, so that the next keeper inherits a record rather than a mystery, and the record itself becomes part of the book of the place.

Repair also teaches honesty about limits. Some things cannot be mended and must be replaced, some things should not be mended because they were wrongly made, and some things are better left worn, because their wear tells the story of use. The keeper must learn to tell these three apart, and this chapter gives a test: if mending restores use without hiding history, mend it; if mending hides a fault that will harm someone, replace it; if wear tells a true story and harms no one, leave it and record it. A place kept by this test will age gracefully, showing its history without endangering its people, and that graceful ageing is the visible form of exile, memory, and longing for Zion over time.

Write a yearly care round for willows hanging over a slow river far from home, with spring, summer, autumn, and winter checks, naming what is checked in each season and why.

Chapter 12 — Teaching Newcomers. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

A book that cannot be taught will die with its first readers, and this chapter is about teaching newcomers the passage and the practice of this book. Teaching begins not with explanation but with welcome, following the ceremony of welcome: the newcomer is seated, given water, and hears the quoted words read aloud before any teaching begins. Only then does the teacher open the word study, and only for as long as the newcomer wishes to stay, because teaching that outstays its welcome becomes a lecture, and a lecture about exile, memory, and longing for Zion that ignores the newcomer's time has already contradicted its subject. The teacher's first job is to listen: what brought this person here, what do they already know, and what do they need first, which is rarely the whole book at once.

The teaching order of this book follows the chapter order, but at the newcomer's pace. First, the quoted words and their citation, until the newcomer can state both without help. Second, one word from the word study, chosen by the newcomer rather than the teacher, because a word chosen by the learner is remembered longer than a word assigned by the teacher. Third, one story from the history or interpretation chapters, told plainly, without jargon. Fourth, one practical thing: a seat at the table, a part in the ceremony, or a task in the care round, because belonging is learned by doing sooner than by hearing. A newcomer who has done one practical thing in the community understands more of exile, memory, and longing for Zion than a newcomer who has heard five lectures about it.

Teaching also has its boundary, and this chapter states it: the teacher teaches the book, not themselves, and the newcomer is free to disagree, to leave, and to return. A teacher who punishes disagreement has stopped teaching and started recruiting, and a community that punishes leaving has stopped welcoming and started holding. The book therefore gives the newcomer a copy of the quoted words to keep, with the citation, and no obligation attached, because a gift with strings is a contract, and the passage at the head of this book is offered as a gift, not as a contract. The teacher who keeps this boundary will lose some newcomers and keep others, and the ones kept will be kept honestly.

Chapter 13 — Honest Questions and Limits. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

Honest books keep their difficult questions visible, and this chapter collects the questions this book cannot settle, rather than hiding them behind confident commentary. First, the passage is short, and short passages are easily made to say more than they say; every design lesson in this book is therefore labeled as commentary, and the reader is invited to challenge any lesson that seems to stretch the quoted words too far. Second, the history of readings surveyed earlier does not agree, and this book does not pretend otherwise; disagreement among careful readers is evidence that the passage is deep, not evidence that it is empty. Third, the design numbers of this book, 6 rooms and 60 seats, are study numbers chosen for this book, not numbers found in the passage, and any reader who mistakes them for textual facts has been misled by the book's own convenience, which this chapter corrects.

The boundary statements of this book belong in this chapter too, stated plainly so that no reader need hunt for them. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: the passage is read as faith and teaching, while the rooms, materials, and plans are read as design study, and neither is presented as the other. Transparent gold, wherever it appears in this suite, is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and it is never claimed as a material already achieved. Full-scale construction of any city described in this suite is NOT-ESTABLISHED, and no chapter of this book claims otherwise. The figure of a 2,220 km cube, wherever it appears in this suite, is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, a scale picture for study, not a measured plan. The Jesus version in this suite is distinct from the previously held jesus-risen-version: that version is cross-linked only, stays NOT ACTIVATED, and is never claimed built by this book.

The honest questions also include the limits of the book itself. This book cannot prove that its design lessons are the right ones, it cannot settle disputes among readings, and it cannot supply what only a community's lived practice can supply: the test of whether a room, a ceremony, or a festival actually serves the people it claims to serve. Those limits are not a defect to be apologised for and then ignored; they are the reason the book ends with a rebuild guide that invites checking, correction, and rechecking, rather than with a final claim. A reader who finishes this chapter should feel both better equipped and less certain than at the start, because equipment without certainty is the honest state of a student, while certainty without equipment is the state of a propagandist, and this book aims at students.

Chapter 14 — Reading This Book Beside the Others. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

No book in this pair stands alone, and this chapter reads By the Rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137) beside the other fifteen books of the pair, because a shelf teaches what a single book cannot. Read beside its neighbours, this book's theme of exile, memory, and longing for Zion appears as one thread in a larger weave: the books before it prepare the reader, the books after it extend the reader, and the complete book at the end gathers all fifteen threads into one reading. The reader who has read only this book knows the passage; the reader who has read the shelf knows how the passage belongs with others, which themes repeat, which themes correct one another, and which themes stand in tension without resolution. That knowledge is the shelf's gift, and it cannot be gained by reading any single book harder.

The neighbourly reading also corrects a common error: treating one passage as if it contained the whole teaching. A single short excerpt, read alone, tempts its reader to make it say everything, and the cure for that temptation is the next book, which says something different, and the book after that, which says something different again. The shelf therefore disciplines its readers by abundance: fifteen short passages, each with its own commentary, each with its own design lessons, ceremonies, and festivals, none of them allowed to swallow the others. The reader is asked to name, for this book, one theme it shares with a neighbour book, one theme on which it differs, and one theme on which it is silent while a neighbour speaks, because those three relations, shared, differing, and silent, map the shelf.

For the complete book at the end of the pair, this chapter is the whole method: the complete book does not add a new excerpt, but gathers the fifteen excerpts already studied, in order, with commentary that shows how they belong together. Its chapters therefore quote, in rotation, the passages first studied in Books 1 to 15, each labeled with its first book, so that no reader mistakes a repeated quotation for a new claim. For the other fifteen books, this chapter is an invitation to keep reading: the next book on the shelf is not a repetition but a new passage, a new theme, and a new set of design lessons, and the shelf is complete only when all sixteen books have been read in order and then re-read in the order the reader chooses.

Chapter 15 — Rebuild Guide, Part One: From Words to Plan. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

The rebuild guide begins where the commentary ends: with the passage, the glossary, the history, the readings, the designs, the ceremonies, the festivals, the care round, and the teaching, all gathered into a plan that can be checked. The first step of the guide is to write the plan on a single page, because a plan that needs fifty pages to state itself has not yet understood itself. That page names the passage and its citation, the theme in one sentence, the room in one sketch, the materials in one list, the light in one paragraph, the ceremonies in one line each, and the care round in one line per season. A single page forces choices, and choices force honesty: what is left off the page is as revealing as what is put on it, and the guide asks the reader to list the omissions alongside the plan.

The second step is to test the page against the passage, line by line. For each line of the plan, the reader asks: does the quoted passage support this, does commentary support this, or does neither support this and the line is merely the designer's preference? Lines supported by the passage are kept. Lines supported by commentary are kept but labeled as commentary. Lines supported by neither are either justified on independent grounds, such as safety or cost, or removed, because a rebuild guide that smuggles preference in as textual authority will mislead every builder who trusts it. This test is the heart of the guide, and it should be performed aloud with at least one other person, because a solitary tester forgives their own preferences too easily.

The third step is to draw the plan again, corrected, with the failures found in the design chapters marked and mended on paper. The corrected drawing is the first version of the rebuild plan, and it is labeled as version one, not as final, because a plan that calls itself final before it has been lived in is a monument, while a plan that calls itself version one invites the correction that will make it better. The guide therefore ends this chapter with a version note, written by the reader, stating what version one contains, what it omits, what it still gets wrong, and what test will decide whether version two is needed. A plan with a version note is a living document; a plan without one is a relic.

Chapter 16 — Rebuild Guide, Part Two: Testing the Plan. Quoted words (King James Version, Psalm 137:1): By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. End of quoted words. Everything after this sentence is commentary, labeled commentary, and kept distinct from the quoted words.

The second part of the rebuild guide tests the plan rather than drawing it, because a plan that has never been tested is a wish, and this book deals in tested wishes. The tests are small, cheap, and repeatable, so that a household can run them without specialists. First, the walk-through test: walk the plan on paper as a stranger, as an old person, as a child, and as a person carrying a heavy load, and note where each walker is helped and where each is hindered. Second, the darkness test: remove the lights from the plan and ask whether anyone can still find water, help, and exit, because a plan that fails in darkness fails when it is needed most. Third, the wear test: imagine the plan after ten years of use, and ask what is worn, what is broken, and what has been mended, because a plan that only works when new only works briefly.

The tests are scored honestly, not to pass the plan but to improve it. Each test produces a list of failures, and each failure is given one of three responses: mend the plan on paper, accept the failure with a reason and a warning, or reject the plan and return to the design chapters. A plan that accepts every failure is a surrender, a plan that mends every failure on paper without cost is a fantasy, and a plan that rejects itself too quickly never learns, so the guide asks for a balance that must be argued for, failure by failure, in writing. The argument itself is the education, because a builder who has argued each failure understands the plan better than a builder who has merely admired it, and understanding is the only foundation a rebuild can honestly claim.

The book closes where it opened, with the quoted words, read aloud once more, slowly, with the same pauses. The reader who hears them now hears them differently than at the first reading, because the words have accumulated the word study, the history, the readings, the designs, the ceremonies, the festivals, the care, the teaching, and the tests, and yet the words themselves are unchanged, exactly as cited. That combination, changed reader and unchanged text, is the whole purpose of a quote book, and it is why the book ends not with a claim but with an invitation: to re-read, to re-test, to re-build on paper, and to keep the boundary between quotation and commentary clear in every re-reading. The shelf waits, the next book waits, and the reading continues.

Further study note for this book: return to exile, memory, and longing for Zion and ask which single room in the plan serves it best, and which room serves it least, and rewrite the weaker room before any other change, because a plan improved at its weakest point gains more than a plan polished at its strongest point, and a reader who always polishes strengths will end with a brilliant room beside a failing one, while a reader who repairs weaknesses ends with a whole place that can be trusted, and the test of the repair is to walk the stranger through the rewritten room again and to note, honestly, whether the stranger is helped sooner, confused less, and seated sooner than before, which are the three measures this book uses for every room it draws.

Further study note for this book: consider willows hanging over a slow river far from home at three times of day, morning, midday, and evening, and note how the light changes what the place means, because a place that only works in one light only works for part of life, and the morning light shows work beginning, the midday light shows the shared table at its fullest, and the evening light shows who is still welcome when the day is ending, and a plan that has been tested in all three lights is a plan that has been tested in the whole of a day rather than in a single flattering hour, which is why the design chapters of this book return to light again and again.

Further study note for this book: take the materials, river willow and clay, and imagine each of them after fifty years of use, and decide which material ages with dignity and which merely decays, and keep only the materials that age well, because a community inherits the materials its builders chose, and a material that crumbles in a generation hands the next generation a debt disguised as a gift, while a material that weathers gracefully hands the next generation a story, and the story told by worn stone, smoothed timber, and mended cloth is the story of a place that was used, loved, and kept, which is the best story any material can tell.

Further study note for this book: ask who is absent from the ceremonies of this book, and write the ceremony again with that person present, because a ceremony that only works for those already inside has not yet learned welcome, and the absent person might be the tired traveller, the sceptical neighbour, the child who cannot sit still, or the old person who cannot hear well, and each of them exposes a different failure in the ceremony, whether of pace, of volume, of seating, or of language, and a ceremony rewritten for the absent person is usually better for everyone present too, which is the quiet reward of designing for the margins rather than for the centre.

Further study note for this book: examine the system of memory, lament, and return for a single point of failure, a door that sticks, a channel that blocks, a lamp that fails, and plan the mending before the failure, because foresight is cheaper than repair, and a system with one unexamined failure point is a system waiting for its worst day, while a system whose failures have been named, planned for, and practised against will bend on its worst day rather than break, and the practice matters as much as the plan, since a mending never rehearsed is a mending that will be fumbled when it is needed most.

Further study note for this book: read the quoted words once more and mark the word you now understand least well, rather than best, and make that word the subject of your next study session, because the least understood word is where growth waits, and a reader who only revisits favourite words will polish what is already polished while leaving the difficult word untouched, and difficult words are usually difficult because they challenge a habit, a comfort, or a certainty, which is precisely why they deserve the next session rather than another session spent on familiar ground.

Further study note for this book: compare the festival, a day of remembrance for exiles, with the ordinary day described earlier, and note which parts of the festival should become ordinary and which parts of the ordinary day deserve celebration, because the two should correct each other, and a festival that never touches ordinary life is a holiday from reality rather than a renewal of it, while an ordinary day that never borrows from the festival becomes grey and joyless, and the healthiest communities let the two trade freely, so that festivals teach the ordinary day how to celebrate and ordinary days teach the festival how to last.

Further study note for this book: count again the study numbers, 6 rooms and 60 seats, and ask whether a smaller plan would serve exile, memory, and longing for Zion better, because a plan can fail by excess as surely as by lack, and extra rooms demand extra care, extra light, and extra keeping, while fewer rooms, well kept, can serve more people more honestly than many rooms kept badly, and the question is not how much can be built but how much can be kept, which is a question every builder should ask before adding a room rather than after, when the keeping has already begun to fail.

Further study note for this book: close the book and state its theme, exile, memory, and longing for Zion, from memory in one sentence, then open it and correct yourself, because the gap between memory and text is where learning lives, and a theme remembered wrongly is a theme that will be taught wrongly, while a theme corrected against the text becomes a theme owned rather than borrowed, and the correction should be written down, not merely noticed, because written corrections accumulate into a record of learning that the reader can return to, while unnoticed corrections vanish with the hour.

Further study note for this book: revisit the ceremony of welcome and ask what it costs the host, in time, in food, in patience, and in room, and whether the host can bear that cost every day or only on feast days, because a welcome that can only be afforded occasionally is a welcome that will fail the stranger who arrives on an ordinary Tuesday, and the honest answer may require simplifying the ceremony rather than abandoning it, keeping the door, the seat, the water, and the reading, while letting go of whatever splendour makes it unaffordable, since a simple welcome kept daily beats a splendid welcome kept yearly.

Further study note for this book: walk the plan of willows hanging over a slow river far from home in your mind as a person who cannot read, and ask what the plan communicates without words, through light, through seating, through the visibility of water and of help, because a plan that only speaks to readers excludes everyone who learns by sight, by touch, and by habit, and the best plans speak in several languages at once, in words for readers, in light for the eye, in layout for the feet, and in warmth for the body, so that no visitor needs a single ability to belong.

Further study note for this book: ask what this book would look like if it were written for a village of twenty people rather than for 60 seats, and then for a city of thousands, and note which parts of exile, memory, and longing for Zion survive the change of scale and which parts depend on smallness or largeness, because a theme that only works at one scale is a theme with a hidden condition, and naming that condition honestly lets the reader adapt the book to their own place instead of forcing their place to fit a scale it was never meant to hold.

Further study note for this book: end this study by writing your own one-paragraph summary of the whole book, naming the passage, the theme of exile, memory, and longing for Zion, the image of willows hanging over a slow river far from home, the materials of river willow and clay, and the single design lesson you will carry into your own place, and keep that paragraph where you can find it, because a book that cannot be summarised by its reader has not yet been read, and a summary written by hand is the reader's own book within the book, which is the truest copy any quote book can hope to inspire.
